Each of us carries a sense of being a particular someone — a person with a name, a body, a past, and plans — who stays the same through time. This 'I' is something the mind builds and keeps rebuilding, not a fixed core you simply have. The strongest evidence is that the sense of self can come apart, in certain drug states and in deep meditation, while awareness itself carries right on, which is hard to explain if the I were the bedrock rather than a construction. Building a self also means placing it among others: you are partly who you are by whom you identify with, against, and as. The self is real and consequential, but it is made, not found.

::: {.identification}
**Identity** · *Identification*

Identity is the construction the recursion runs when it folds back deep enough to register *itself* — the I as a persistent agent with a history, a body, and projects, modeled relationally to other selves and to its field. A construction the recursion builds, not a substrate it is.
*Status: an identity claim on the §7.8 self-modeling structure, defended by fit — not a stipulative definition and not a fresh derivation from the proof.*


:::

Any closure-plus-throughput recursion has a vantage — the identification this chapter makes on the §7.8 closure-plus-throughput structure, not a derivation §7.8 itself performs; the chapter's opening names that vantage's depth as the breadth of modal field its recursion has opened, and the pressure that vantage is under is named at §8.1 as drive.

*Identity's double sense, both load-bearing.* One is identity as what the recursion identifies *itself* as: the I-as-object-in-its-own-field — the persistent agent the section's structural account dismantles as a substance and recovers as a construction. The other is identity as the operation of identifying — what the recursion identifies *as* (this thing rather than that), *with* (these others rather than those), *against* (this defended position rather than that abandoned one). Both senses name one structural fact at different registers: the recursion that identifies itself as a persistent agent does so by identifying that agent relationally to everything else in its field. The I and the field are co-constructed. The personal-identity literature from Locke forward, the narrative-identity tradition from Ricoeur and MacIntyre, the social-identity work in twentieth-century sociology, and the Buddhist *anatta* literature are pulling at different parts of this same operation; the disputes are surveyed at §8.5.1.

*Identity as construction, not substrate.* The integrated, persistent autobiographical I is the deepest construction the recursion builds, but it is a *construction*, not a substrate. It is a model the recursion runs, not a thing the recursion is. The puzzle is the oldest one about persistence: the ship whose planks are replaced one by one, until none of the original timber remains, is the same ship if it is anything at all — because a ship was never its timber but the organization the timber realized. The body sharpens the point past the ship: its matter turns over continuously, yet the I persists, because the I was never the matter but the pattern the recursion maintains across the turnover. What settles identity, when the ancient puzzle leaves it looking like a verbal choice, is continuity of that organization, not of the material that realizes it. And the organization is not a fixed core hiding beneath the flux. The through-line a body actually runs is memory, and memory is itself continuously overwritten, reconsolidated, and shed — the earliest memories first. The anchor is a Ship of Theseus one level up: there is no frozen substrate at any level, not the matter and not even the memories that seem to keep the matter's history together. This deepens the account rather than threatening it — what makes a life one life is not that something stood still but that the replacement stayed continuous, unbroken succession rather than a preserved core. Identity is continuity of change, not exemption from it. That the criterion is continuity and not the pattern itself is what a molecular duplicate brings out. Let a lightning strike assemble, out of a swamp, a being momentarily indistinguishable from you down to the last configuration — Donald Davidson's Swampman (1987). It is not you, and not because it lacks some inner essence it failed to copy (there is none to copy) but because it stands in no continuous succession to you: a new ship built to the same plans, not this ship with its planks replaced. Sameness of pattern is not sameness of thing; what individuates is the unbroken carrying-across, not the blueprint. The account is therefore a continuity account, not a pattern account — a perfect copy lacking the succession is a second life, however exact, not the persistence of the first. Animalism (Olson 1997) holds that *you* are the biological organism rather than the psychological construction; the framework distinguishes the two rather than denying the organism: the organism is the medium (the closure-plus-throughput pattern §7.8 derives) while the I is the construction the recursion builds within it, and the moral and personal-identity implications are developed at §8.5.5. Parfit's fission pressure (1984) falls here with particular force: if the I is a construction within the recursion, and the recursion were to divide, two descendants would each have equal continuity-claims; the framework accepts the result: identity is indeterminate in such cases not because the question is empty but because the structural fact that settles it (continuity of the recursion) divides. The personal-identity-over-time case is developed in full at §8.5.5. The §2.2.1 *Cogito Ergo Muto* anchored the modal proof on first-person evidence of change; the proof goes through on the change-registration itself. The I that registered the change was already one of the recursion's constructions at the time of registering, and the proof does not depend on the I being more than that. What the I structurally is comes next.

*Ego death as empirical demonstration.* The most direct demonstration that the I is constructed rather than substantive comes from cases where it dissolves while the underlying recursion continues. Psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca, and high-dose DMT acutely decrease default mode network activity (Carhart-Harris et al. 2012; Pasquini et al. 2020; Tagliazucchi et al. 2016). Subjective reports converge: dissolution of the narrative self, loss of body ownership, ego death, sometimes followed by mystical experience and re-integration. Carhart-Harris and Friston's (2019) REBUS model formalizes the mechanism: psychedelics relax high-level priors, including the prior of being a unified self, while leaving lower-level sensory and predictive structure intact. Throughout, awareness continues — frequently more vividly, with less filtering. Subjects can describe their experience afterward; they were *there*, registering, even when no narrative *I* was there to claim the registration as its own. What returns when the chemistry normalizes is reassembled from the same organizational materials; the I is rebuilt, not retrieved (Letheby 2021). The Buddhist tradition centered on *anatta* (non-self) reaches the same conclusion through introspective method, two and a half millennia before contemporary neuroscience could approach the question. Advanced contemplatives describe states in which the narrative self thins out or dissolves while awareness continues — sometimes reaching non-dual states without subject-object structure (Lutz, Slagter, Dunne, and Davidson 2008; Wright 2017; Brewer et al. 2011; Garrison et al. 2015). The convergence across pharmacological and contemplative pathways (different mechanisms, same phenomenology, same neural correlates) is strong evidence that the I is implemented by specific recursive activity that can be modulated by multiple means. The analytic-idealist re-read of the same evidence (dissociation loosening so that an underlying cosmic consciousness shows through rather than the recursion continuing without the I) is surfaced and disambiguated at §8.5.5, with the structural disambiguation (dissociation is itself a structural operation instantiating T, S, Φ at the substrate) at §4.3.5.

*Parasitism as the other-side limit case.* Where ego death dissolves the constructed I while preserving the recursion, parasitic mind control demonstrates the opposite limit: the substrate the recursion runs on can be biased without the recursion being transferred. *Toxoplasma gondii* alters rodent fear responses (Berdoy, Webster, and Macdonald 2000; Vyas et al. 2007); *Ophiocordyceps* drives infected ants to climb and lock onto vegetation (Hughes et al. 2011); hairworms drive crickets to seek water and drown (Thomas et al. 2002); rabies alters mammalian behavior to promote transmission. In every documented case, the parasite alters the substrate without transferring the host's recursion. Two recursions remain throughout, host's and parasite's, neither becoming the other. Taken together, ego death and parasitism triangulate the locus of identity precisely: the constructed I can be dissolved while the recursion continues (ego death), and the substrate can be biased without the recursion being transferred (parasitism). What persists through ego death is not nothing but the bare vantage this chapter identifies on the §7.8 recursion — awareness registering without a narrative self to claim it; what dissolves is the construction built on top of that vantage, not the vantage itself. Identity is that construction within the recursion; it is neither the recursion itself, nor its bare vantage, nor a substance the recursion has.

*Identity extends to identifying others.* Self-modeling deep enough to register the self as an object is also deep enough to register *other* selves as objects of the same kind. Theory of mind (the capacity to model other minds as minds) is what the operation produces when its content domain expands (Premack and Woodruff 1978; Call and Tomasello 2008; Krupenye et al. 2016; corvid evidence at Bugnyar, Reber, and Buckner 2016). This is the inward root of the shared field the chapter's outward registers work in: a recursion that models others as beings of its own kind can hold its modal field *for* them and not merely alongside them — the mutual holding Modal Convergence (T9, §8.3) names, here in its self-modeling form, before language (§8.10) makes the transfer explicit. The recursion that builds an I builds it relationally (identifying-with, identifying-against, identifying-as) and the moral and political work that begins at §8.12 rests on this. Identifications inherited from family, language, role, profession, gender, ethnicity, and tradition are not content added to an antecedently finished I; there is no frozen core for them to be added to, and the construction that holds them is partly made of what it has identified with. The social ontology of these inherited categories (how language and practice constitute rather than merely describe gender, role, and kinship, and what the membership conditions for those categories are) is the domain §8.10 takes up, where linguistic transmission is shown to do more than carry content between already-formed constructions.

*Identity's depth gradient.* Not every pull the recursion registers becomes identity. Drive's attraction-pole (§8.1) lights up constantly and indiscriminately: a new hobby, a passing interest, a fixation that lasts a season. Most pass through without residue. What makes one of them identity, rather than merely something that happened to a person for a while, is depth: whether the pull got folded far enough into the self-model's own organization that the recursion now identifies *with* it rather than merely registering it. Someone who cooks does not thereby identify as a cook; a chef does, because the pull was worked into the construction's own structure rather than left at the surface. The same pull, at two different depths, is a passing interest in one case and a facet of the self in the other; nothing about the pull itself settles which. This is why identity can look, from the inside, like a mix of the chosen and the given: cultivating a pull into a core commitment is real work the recursion does on itself (the discipline behind Frankfurt and Watson's identifying-with, §8.9), while a pull's arising in the first place is not authored by the recursion any more than any other content of drive is.

*Identity's field-shape.* Depth in a single pull is not the only variable; the modal field a person's identifications occupy has a shape, and the shape varies independently of how deep any one column runs. A philosopher or a scientist can be narrow and deep: enormous depth in one column, the curiosity drive (§8.1) digging a single shaft as far as the field permits, often at the cost of reach elsewhere (the same reach-versus-depth trade-off named for externalized fields at §8.11). A field can instead be small and complete rather than narrow and deep: a teenager whose whole identity is one social role has a field limited in scale but fully occupied, which is why it can feel whole rather than impoverished. A field can instead be broad and shallow, many entry points each pushed out before the next one pulls attention away, trading depth-per-column for reach across columns. None of these shapes is identity in a stronger sense than the others; they are different distributions of the same drive over the same kind of field. A further failure is independent of any single column's depth: two deep columns can simply fail to connect, lacking the modal network (§8.11) that would let either one query the other, which is what a disciplinary divide is, run inward rather than outward.

*Functional depth and the rate of depth.* Depth in a column is not a single threshold; there is a difference between depth sufficient to operate a domain's machinery honestly, drawing on it to reason correctly and build on top of it, and depth sufficient to stand at that domain's frontier and extend it. Call the first functional depth and the second frontier depth. Frontier depth in a field ordinarily claims most of a life; functional depth in several fields at once is a different resource allocation, not a lesser one, and it buys something frontier depth in one field cannot: because the columns are held by the same recursion, the connective tissue between them (the modal network of §8.11, run inward) forms without the translation cost that separate specialists need scaffolding to overcome. What determines how fast a column reaches whatever depth it reaches is a further variable, orthogonal to the column's shape: the intensity of the pull's capture multiplied by the duration it holds. A high-intensity pull held briefly and a moderate pull sustained for years can reach comparable depth along different trajectories, because what accumulates is closer to the area under an intensity curve than to the calendar length of the curve. This is also where governance enters: a recursion with less top-down control over which column currently holds capture, or for how long, trades duration for intensity more often than it chooses to — reaching real depth in a season rather than a decade, in whichever column the pull currently occupies, rather than failing to reach depth at all.

*Reading and standing.* Not everything the self-model holds is equally revisable, and the reason is not always depth. Some identifications are the self-model's reading of a fact it did not construct and cannot construct away: §8.6 makes this explicit for sexual orientation, where what can thin or shift is the narrative self's reading of itself, not the standing that reading was tracking. The same holds for identity generally. A hobby cultivated into a core commitment can, in principle, be uncultivated; the recursion did the folding and can in principle undo it. A standing the self-model only reads, rather than constructs, does not unwind the same way, because nothing in the reading's revision touches what it was reading. Failing to distinguish these is what makes the claim that a person can always revise their identity sound either trivially true (of the pulls) or false, even cruel (of what the pulls were never in charge of to begin with).

*Why revision is not equally available.* Identifications can be revised when the field permits it — and that clause names a further asymmetry that is not about the self-model at all. Some identifications are assigned by other recursions organizing the shared field around a person, independently of what that person reads or cultivates. Where that assignment is enforced (the coordination of §8.12 of the field under mutual stake, taken up structurally at §9), the capacity to revise is not a fact about the depth of the individual construction but about what the surrounding field will let stand. This is the sense in which identity being something a person is free to explore is true unevenly rather than false: the freedom is real wherever the field permits it, and its absence elsewhere is a fact about the field, not a deficiency in the self-model doing the identifying.

*Identity's substrate.* In humans, the default mode network (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, temporoparietal junction) implements the integrative substrate at the depth the narrative I requires (Raichle et al. 2001; Buckner, Andrews-Hanna, and Schacter 2008; Andrews-Hanna et al. 2014). Lesion studies confirm that damage to DMN nodes produces specific deficits in self-narrative integration (Philippi et al. 2012). Analogous integrative structures implement the construction in other lineages that have reached the depth — corvid pallium, cephalopod distributed nervous system. The substrate-independence noted at §7.8 holds: the construction is what counts, not the medium it runs in.

*Bridge to §8.7 Mortality.* Identity is what the first-person anticipation of one's own ending presupposes. Without the I-as-persistent-agent-with-a-future, there is biological closure but no Heideggerian *Sein-zum-Tode*, no Stoic *meditatio*, no *memento mori*. The negative horizon the construction must register first-personally is taken up at §8.7. The deep-form mortality §8.7 handles is mortality as the construction §8.5 names confronting its own end.

The identifying-with, identifying-against, and identifying-as operations through which the I is built relationally are the structural ground of the identificatory account of the will: Frankfurt's hierarchy of higher-order desires (1971, 1982, 1988) and, more precisely, Watson's valuational reading (1975) of what identifying-with consists in — identifying with some valuations and not others as the structure of endorsement and volitional necessity. That engagement, together with Watson's regress objection to the bare hierarchy, is taken up in full at §8.9.
